extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor, writers, playwrights and comedians interested in theoretical principles of the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and characterizing what produces the comic in human forms, gestures, social rites and language, with practical examples drawn from theatre, clowning and literature. The page gives conceptual laws and exemplars for producing or identifying laughable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast with gracefulness / rigidness vs. gracefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic contrasts with gracefulness more than with ugliness: it partakes of rigidness rather than mere unsightliness. Where matter dulls the outward life of the soul, petrifies movements and thwarts gracefulness, it achieves a comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on situations where the body's materiality resists the soul's suppleness — permanent grimaces, stereotyped attitudes, or cramped movements. Example: a face frozen into an intended grimace becomes its own caricature. The comic is linked to immobility or contracture imposed on living variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudes, gestures and movements are laughable in proportion as the body reminds us of a mere machine
rubrics_metrics.description: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The suggestion must be both clear (we perceive a set-up mechanism within the person) and subtle (the person still appears living). Comic artists succeed when they make a person and a machine fit into each other closely while retaining a trace of life — e.g., a jointed puppet impression in a living figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / automatism in gesture causes laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement always the same, recurring at regular intervals, evokes laughter because it makes us see a machine working automatically — automatism established in life and imitating it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeated identical gestures in speakers or performers; if audience members can 'wait for it' and then laugh when it occurs, the effect is mechanical. Comic technique: intentionally repeat a neutral gesture to suggest internal automatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation exposes mechanical uniformity and increases laughability
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures become laughable when imitated because imitation brings out the mechanical uniformity that the original person allowed to creep into their behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation highlights what is alien to living personality; parody should connect gestures to simple mechanical occupations (sawing wood, tugging a bell-rope) to make them seem intentionally mechanical. Hence imitation and parody amplify comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical interpretation of gestures (deflection toward simple operations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures become more laughable when they are deflected, without altering form, toward some mechanical occupation; this makes the incriminated gesture seem more frankly mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A favourite device of parody: reinterpret a speaker's gesture as if it were part of sawing wood, striking an anvil, etc., to emphasize automatism. The comic increases when the audience can plausibly map a gesture onto a simple machine-like operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform multiplicity (many similar actors/gestures) creates a marionette hallucination
rubrics_metrics.description: When several people behave in the same way simultaneously—striking same attitudes, tossing arms alike—absolute uniformity makes them seem like marionettes joined by invisible threads; litheness stiffens into automatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crowds or choruses repeating identical movements to produce mechanical hallucination; theatrical choreography that multiplies sameness heightens comic perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage devices derive comic force by suggesting a clockwork arrangement while preserving probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices like periodical repetition of a word/scene, systematic inversion, geometrical development of misunderstanding, etc., draw comic force from setting before us an obvious clockwork arrangement of human events while keeping an outward aspect of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should craft sequences that hint at mechanical causation but keep them plausible enough that the audience still sees living causes — the tension produces laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise and fashion: sudden dissolution of continuity revives latent comic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A garment or fashion becomes laughable when it is so incompatible with the person that the usual fusion of dress and wearer is broken; similarly, sudden changes (e.g., hair colour, a red nose) are treated by imagination as disguises and appear comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic arises not simply from surprise or contrast but from the perception that something customarily fused with a person is now an external disguise. Authors can exploit temporal discontinuities in dress or appearance to reveal latent comic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination's logic treats surface alterations as disguise (imaginary masquerade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination often treats inherent traits (a red nose, a black face) as if they were artificial coatings or disguises; this 'logic of imagination'—distinct from reason—produces comic associations of masquerade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that comic perception can rest on culturally shared imaginative habits; what shocks the habitual continuity (colour, ornament) will be read as makeup/disguise and thus become laughable. Beware: continuity/custom can deaden comic effect until disrupted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature mechanically tampered with is faintly comic; closer resemblance to mechanical tampering strengthens the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where nature is suggested as disguised or tampered with (half-clipped dog, artificially coloured flowers, plastered trees) are comic because they recall masquerade; stronger comic effects arise when one contrasts these with the original source (mechanical tampering of life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imaginative amplification (e.g., an artificially manufactured Switzerland) to make the mechanical intervention in nature salient. The more explicitly the reader/viewer perceives artificial manufacture, the stronger the comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony/formulaic social actions contain latent comic element (form over matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial and stereotyped social actions are laughable when isolated from their serious ends; they give the impression of puppets obeying a formula—form replacing matter and becoming automatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the ceremonial aspect while neglecting its matter/serious aim (e.g., prize-distribution, solemn court sitting). Examples: officials performing rules at an inappropriate moment ('Anything to declare?') creates comic incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of artificial/administrative regulation for natural law produces comic pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: When human regulations or pedantry usurp the place of natural or moral law, the result is comic—an administrative enactment occupying the relation to nature that a garment does to a living body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirize bureaucratic formalism, pedantry and the mechanical application of rules that ignore human realities. Example: a philosopher claiming 'Experience is in the wrong' — a comic inversion of common-sense relation between theory and reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any incident is comic that calls attention to the physical when the moral side is concerned (body precedence over soul)
rubrics_metrics.description: ANY INCIDENT IS COMIC THAT CALLS OUR ATTENTION TO THE PHYSICAL IN A PERSON WHEN IT IS THE MORAL SIDE THAT IS CONCERNED. The body tantalised by needs, or a person embarrassed by his body, yields laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bodily distractions in tragedy; in comedy, exploit them—e.g., a speaker sneezing at a pathetic moment, a hero sitting down during an eloquent speech. Use physical interruptions to undercut moral or rhetorical seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner seeking to outdo matter / profession ridiculed when form outweighs function
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often arises when manner (form, procedure) seeks to outdo matter (substance, purpose): professions appear ridiculous when their external formalities are scrupulously respected while their ends are neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray professionals as devoted to ritual and appearance rather than outcomes (doctors preferring rules to cure). This substitution creates professional automatism, ripe for ridicule—pair it with physical overtones to amplify effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical defects as overtones to intellectual/moral ossification
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic 'overtones' naturally attach to a fundamental note: intellectual ossification is often complemented by physical peculiarity (stammer, stutter, slow speech) which prepares the audience to perceive moral infirmity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/actors should match physical peculiarities of speech or movement to the character's intellectual or moral rigidity to make the ridicule feel psychologically coherent. If the playwright omits it, actors may invent such defects instinctively.

rubrics_metrics.name: We laugh when a person gives us the impression of being a thing (person → thing transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING. Examples: Sancho Panza tumbled like a football, clowns becoming rubber balls or wooden dummies through repeated, accelerating rebounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce scenes where bodies are gradually perceived as objects by intensifying repetition, acceleration, rounding of forms, and crescendo in action. Clowning techniques (rebound, exaggerated rigidity, successive heavier impacts) are textbook examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion and rhythmical devices to induce comic hallucination
rubrics_metrics.description: The best comic suggestions often work by gradual passing from vague to distinct impressions (suggestion par excellence), and by lulling imagination through arrangement of rhythm, rhyme and assonance to prepare it to accept a comic image (e.g., a doll).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke the comic subtly, use incremental hints and rhythmic/sonic patterns that rock the imagination between like and like, making an improbable image (person as doll/thing) acceptable. This is a poetic/performative technique for generating laughter.
